newsitem.title: USA: Iraq's Saddam not to be trusted - U.S. admiral.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Saddam not to be trusted - U.S. admiral.

text.p: The commander of U.S. warships in the Gulf said on Saturday Iraq's Saddam Hussein was not to be trusted despite Baghdad's pledge to halt attacks against U.S. aircraft policing southern and northern Iraq.

The Iraqi president "has a track record of saying one thing and doing another," Rear-Admiral Edward Moore told visiting reporters as U.S. jets flew off the carrier to patrol the no-fly zone over southern Iraq.

Iraq on Friday night withdrew an earlier vow, saying it would no longer shoot at U.S. and allied aircraft in the zones that are off-limits to Iraqi aircraft. Baghdad has never formally recognised the zones, which were established by Kuwait's Western allies after the 1991 Gulf War.

"Saddam Hussein has said he will not shoot at our aircraft any more...The proclamation was made after we stopped flying last night...So we will have to wait and see whether he will or not" fire at the Western aircraft, said Moore.
Iraq's firing of a missile on Wednesday at two U.S. planes in the northern zone triggered a big American build-up in the oil-rich region for possible wider strikes against Iraq.
Earlier last week the U.S. fired 44 cruise missiles at targets in the south in retaliation for Iraq's military role in factional Kurdish fighting in the north of the country.
The admiral said that out at sea it was difficult to know if tension was rising or if the situation was defusing but "I think the tensions (with Iraq) are about in a steady stage right now."

Moore's naval task force of about 23 warships will be joined soon by an additional 7,500 sailors and about 90 warplanes on board six warships -- three of which are capable of firing Tomahawk cruise missiles.
The aircraft carrier USS Enterprise battle group, which includes a submarine, is heading to the region to join the Vinson battle group, which also has a submarine.
Naval sources said orders from Washington to the task force were constantly changing, but the Vinson could lay anchor at sea on Sunday for maintenance work.

Earlier in the day the commander of the Vinson said the carrier, on duty in the Gulf since July 1, might carry out maintenance work at sea while some of the more than 5,000 sailors onboard hold a "steel beach picnic" on the flight deck.
But "I can get underway (for combat mission) at a moment's notice," said Captain Larry Baucom as the carrier moved to within 200 km (120 miles) off Iraq.
Navy officials later said the some 75 warplanes on board the carrier and its weapons would be immediately ready for combat if the maintenance order is reversed.
"War is not what we are here for but if it comes to that we are ready," said Electronic Warfare (EW) aircraft pilot Curte Pope, from Mooreland, Indiana.
